newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Unocal wants Turkmen-Pakistan gas link into India.
newsitem.headline: Unocal wants Turkmen-Pakistan gas link into India.

text.p: Unocal Corp of the United States hopes to extend a planned Turkmenistan-Pakistan gas pipeline into northern India, since Pakistani gas demand may fall short of targets, a company official said on Thursday.
"The market for the gas (in Pakistan) is substantial, but not as great as we originally thought," said Chris Taggart, executive vice-president of Unocal unit Unocal International Energy Ventures.
"An extension of the pipeline to India would greatly strengthen the market (for the gas)," he said in a speech to the Turkmenistan International Oil and Gas 1997 Projects Conference.
Unocal said Turkmenistan and Pakistan had officially recognised the company as consortium leader for the pipeline project.
Unocal plans to build a pipeline from the Turkmen-Afghan border to Multan in northern Pakistan and possibly on to Sikandra Rao, just east of New Delhi in India.
The extension into India would add another $600 million to the cost of the project.
The pipeline from Turkmenistan to Multan is expected to cost $1.9 billion, Taggart said.
But it will complicate clearance of the project at governmental level, he said, adding, "we know (the extension) won't be easy."
However, the economics of extending the pipeline would be favourable longer term, Taggart said.
The idea of extending the pipeline into India is not new, but the latest analysis of likely demand in northern Pakistan for the gas made it more desirable, he said.
Taggart estimated Pakistani demand for gas running through the pipeline at 12.4 billion cubic metres (bcm) annually, against planned pipeline capacity of 20.0 bcm.
"This demand can be expected within a reasonable timeframe, and is probably sufficient for the project," he said.
The pipeline would run across Afghanistan, where political instability threatens delays.
The radical Islamic Taleban militia captured the Afghan capital Kabul last September and now control over three quarters of Afghanistan.
Unocal officials were careful not to predict when they thought Afghanistan would be stable enough to allow the plan to proceed.

"Agreements are unpredictable," Taggart said. "They require not only an internationally-recognised government in Afghanistan, but an internationally- recognised government in Afghanistan that we can do business with," he said.
"I can't predict how long this will take."
Turkmenistan is keen for a quick start-up to the project, which once begun would take around two years to complete.

The pipeline would pump gas transported by Turkmenistan to the Afghan border from the huge Dauletabad field, which has been in production since 1983. The consortium would buy the gas at the Turkmen-Afghan border and market it to Asia.

Now Turkmenistan relies entirely on the Russian gas pipeline system to get its gas to markets, and limited space is capping production of what is the most important hard-currency earner for the former Soviet republic.
Consortium members so far are Unocal, Delta Oil Co of Saudi Arabia, Gazprom of Russia, and Turkmenrusgaz, a company joining Gazprom and Turkmen state enterprises.
